summary: Collects current definitions for many terms used in the DNS, which is spread over dozens of RFCs whose terminology has shifted over the years. It was replaced by RFC 8499.

eli5.summary: This is a glossary for the Internet's phone book. It was replaced by RFC 8499.

questions: where can i find dns terminology
subtitle: A glossary of DNS terms clarified after decades of shifting definitions.

tldr.problem: DNS is spread across dozens of RFCs whose terminology has changed over the decades, causing confusion among practitioners.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7719 collects and defines current DNS terminology in one place, noting where new consensus definitions differ from the original RFCs.
tldr.outcome: This document was replaced by RFC 8499, which provides an even more comprehensive DNS terminology resource.

today: RFC 7719 has been obsoleted by RFC 8499, which provides an updated and more comprehensive DNS terminology glossary.

sections.title: Introduction to DNS Terminology
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) has evolved across dozens of RFCs since its original definition in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 in 1987. The terminology used by DNS implementers, developers, and operators has shifted significantly over these decades. Terms that were precisely defined in early RFCs have taken on new meanings, while newer terms have emerged from the community without formal definitions.

RFC 7719 brings together current definitions for the terminology used in DNS. Most are the consensus definitions agreed upon by the DNS community. Where definitions have evolved, the RFC notes the differences from earlier RFCs. Some terms appear here despite never having been formally defined in any RFC before.

It is important to recognize that DNS terminology itself is not entirely consistent even within this document. Different DNS experts may interpret some terms differently, and some definitions have shifted so much from their origins that understanding context is essential when reading older RFCs.
sections.eli5: Think of DNS like a big organization that has been around for a long time. Different people wrote different rules about it, and the words they used have changed. This document explains what all those words mean right now.

sections.title: Names and Domain Structure
sections.content:
DNS organizes names in a tree structure where each node has a label (0 to 63 octets). A domain name is the list of labels from a node to the root, and the total length cannot exceed 255 octets. A fully qualified domain name (FQDN) technically includes the zero-length root label at the end (written with a trailing dot: www.example.net.), but names are often written relative to the root and still called fully qualified.

A host name is typically a domain name that follows the preferred name syntax rules (letters, digits, and hyphens), though the definition has drifted over time. A Top-Level Domain (TLD) is a zone one layer below the root, such as com or jp. A subdomain is a domain contained within another domain; for example, mmm.example.com and nnn.mmm.example.com are both subdomains of example.com.

Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) use the IDNA protocol to handle non-ASCII characters. A public suffix is a domain under which subdomains can be registered and on which HTTP cookies should not be set (like com.au). There is no technical way to identify a public suffix from a domain name alone; lists are maintained externally.
sections.eli5: A domain name is like an address in a postal system. Each part is a label, and there is a special root at the top. Some names are first names of computers (host names), some are major zones like .com (TLDs), and some are just subdomains under others.

sections.title: DNS Servers and Clients
sections.content:
A resolver extracts information from name servers in response to client requests. In practice, there are several types. A stub resolver cannot perform full resolution itself and depends on a recursive resolver to do the actual work. A full-service resolver acts in recursive mode with a cache and meets other requirements defined in RFC 1123.

An authoritative server knows the content of a DNS zone from local knowledge and answers queries about that zone with the AA (authoritative answer) flag set. An authoritative-only server serves only authoritative data and ignores recursive requests. A secondary server uses zone transfer to retrieve zone data from a primary server. The terms slave and master, used in early RFCs, have fallen out of favor in modern usage.

A forwarder resolves queries instead of using the authoritative nameserver chain, typically because it has better Internet access or maintains a shared cache. A policy-implementing resolver changes some answers based on policy (such as blocking malware sites). An open resolver or public resolver accepts queries from any stub resolver.

A view is a DNS server configuration that provides different answers depending on query attributes such as source IP address. This feature is widely implemented but is not standardized in the DNS protocol.
sections.eli5: Some computers answer DNS questions (servers), and some computers ask them (clients). Some servers know the real answers (authoritative), and some just pass the question along (recursive). Some servers have helpers that do parts of the work.

sections.title: Zones and Resource Records
sections.content:
A zone is a unit of authoritative information that can be automatically distributed to redundant servers. The apex is the point in the tree where an SOA and authoritative NS records exist. A zone cut is the boundary where one zone ends and a child zone begins. A delegation is the process of creating a separate zone by adding an NS record set in the parent zone.

Glue records are address records included in a parent zone to provide the addresses of name servers in delegated child zones. Without glue, a resolver might need to know the address to learn the address, creating a circular problem. Records are classified as in-bailiwick or out-of-bailiwick depending on whether the server is authoritative for them.

A resource record is the basic unit of DNS data. An RRset is a set of resource records with the same label, class, and type but different data; all must have the same TTL. The TTL is the maximum time a record can be cached. A zone transfer copies zone data using AXFR for full transfer or IXFR for incremental transfer.

Empty non-terminals are domain names that own no resource records but have subdomains that do. A wildcard is an resource record with an owner name starting with an asterisk that can synthesize RRs for matching names. A CNAME is a resource record that aliases a name to a canonical name, though the term is often misused to refer to the owner name itself.
sections.eli5: A zone is a section of the DNS tree that one person is in charge of. Records are the actual facts stored in DNS. Some tricks make zones work: glue records help you find the name servers, wildcards match many names at once, and aliases point one name to another.

sections.title: DNSSEC and Secure Lookups
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses. A signed zone contains properly constructed DNSKEY, RRSIG, and NSEC or NSEC3 records. An unsigned zone does not include these records or cannot be validated by a security-aware resolver.

A validating resolver can determine one of four states for a response. Secure means a chain of trust from a trust anchor to the RRset. Insecure means no chain of trust but proof that the zone is intentionally unsigned. Bogus means a chain of trust exists but signatures fail to validate. Indeterminate means no trust anchor established.

DNSSEC uses two types of keys: Key Signing Keys that sign the apex DNSKEY RRset, and Zone Signing Keys that sign other RRsets. When these roles are combined, the key is called a Combined Signing Key. The Secure Entry Point flag marks keys intended as trust anchors. NSEC and NSEC3 records provide authenticated denial of existence. NSEC3 also supports Opt-Out, which allows unsigned delegations to be covered by a single NSEC3 record and zone enumeration mitigation.
sections.eli5: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS answers so you can prove they are real. Zones can be signed (trustworthy) or unsigned (you cannot prove them). Special keys protect the signatures, and special records prove that something does not exist.
